title: How Motion Sickness Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore motion sickness: personal anecdotes (Body Wars ride at Disney World, car reading, a cruise), risk factors such as age between two and twelve, sex differences tied to body weight distribution, pregnancy, migraines, poor sleep, and genetics (twin and parent studies, a Penn State study on Asian participants). They cover the sensory conflict theory, the sway theory proposed by a University of Minnesota kinesiology professor, Michael Eaton's toxin-based explanation for nausea, and landsickness (mal de debarquement). They then review prevention and remedies: looking at the horizon, fresh air, seat position, diet, ginger and other herbs, acupressure wristbands, scopolamine, homeopathy, biofeedback and habituation exercises. The episode closes with a listener mail story about a bonsai demonstration.

segments.title: Opening banter and personal motion sickness stories
segments.summary: Hosts swap stories about getting carsick from reading, a Body Wars ride at Disney World that made Josh sick, and a cruise. They joke about Josh's brother and Avatar.

segments.title: Risk factors and who gets motion sick
segments.summary: Common risk factors are listed, including age between two and twelve, puberty, sex differences, pregnancy, menstruation, migraines, and poor sleep. Studies on Asian participants and twins are discussed, with genetics suggested but not proven.

segments.title: Motion sickness test devices and amusement park rides
segments.summary: The hosts describe the optokinetic drum and a chair used to induce motion sickness in studies, and a former Six Flags Over Georgia barrel ride. They discuss a legend about a girl whose ponytail was caught in a ride.

segments.title: Sensory conflict theory
segments.summary: The sensory conflict theory is explained: the eyes, inner ear vestibular system, and body sensors send conflicting signals, as when watching a flying scene while seated. Avatar is used as an example.

segments.title: Sway theory and the sex difference explanation
segments.summary: Thomas Stoffregen's sway theory holds that motion sickness arises when movement contradicts the natural swaying of standing upright. Sway differs by sex after puberty because of where body weight sits, hips for women and chest for men. The hosts question why sway would cause nausea.
topics: center of gravity and sex differences

segments.title: Toxin theory of nausea and landsickness
segments.summary: Michael Eaton's explanation is described: the body mistakes vestibular disruption for toxin exposure and vomits to expel it. Landsickness is then covered, where the brain still perceives movement after returning to land.

segments.title: Prevention tips and remedies
segments.summary: Advice includes keeping eyes on the horizon, keeping the head still, avoiding heavy meals and alcohol, getting fresh air, sitting in the front of planes or over the wing, and avoiding salty foods. Remedies covered include ginger, peppermint, acupressure wristbands, scopolamine, and homeopathy.

segments.title: Biofeedback, habituation, and driver tip
segments.summary: Biofeedback and relaxation training helped fifty pilots return to flying, according to a study described. Sam Puma's habituation exercises are mentioned, and the hosts suggest pretending to drive to avoid motion sickness as a passenger.

segments.title: Listener mail: bonsai demonstration
segments.summary: A listener named Nancy Gallagher describes a bonsai master beating a root ball with a club during a college class visit. The hosts also mention Pat Morita.
